newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA rebels take aim at France after arrests.
newsitem.headline: ETA rebels take aim at France after arrests.

text.p: France's increased cooperation with Spain against the Basque separatist group ETA has prompted the rebels to make a radical switch to bring high-profile French targets into their sights, Spanish officials said on Friday.

ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which usually strikes in Spain, put French Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre and his predecessor Charles Pasqua on a list of possible targets found during a raid by French police.
The list was in a cache of documents police uncovered when they arrested suspected Basque rebel leader Juan Luis Aguirre Lete on Tuesday, a justice source said.
The French targets mean a big shift in tactics for the guerrillas, who have seen the Spanish state as the number one enemy in their 28-year struggle for Basque independence.

"This would signify an escalation, a radical change in the strategy of ETA," Interior Ministry spokesman Fernando Delgado told Reuters. "If it were true, it would cause us great pain that they (French officials) were being persecuted with us."
Spain earlier applauded France's arrest of Aguirre Lete, saying it had averted "certain bloodshed" by leading to the dismantling of an ETA squad planning attacks in the partly Basque Navarre region.

The Civil Guard arrested two men -- Pedro Zubizarreta, 25, and Igor Miguel Angulo, 23 -- and seized a sizeable arsenal that included long-range precision assault rifles, bomb-making materials, detonators, and false identity papers.
The men, identified in documents found by French police, were believed to be part of the squad that attacked a Civil Guard barracks with a car bomb on November 1 and injured five.
Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said the squad, which had been dismantled by police once before, had been re-formed with plans for a widescale assault in the Navarre.
"These arrests have been possible thanks to the documents seized by the French police as a result of the recent detentions in our neighbouring country," he said in a statement.
"They have averted, without a doubt, numerous criminal activities that the terrorist group had planned."

Spanish officials said France may have become vulnerable because its cosier relations with Madrid's young conservative administration, which replaced a 13-year Socialist government in May, had led to more bilateral police cooperation and success.
The conservative governments of the two countries have met four times since Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar took office and bilateral relations are "better than before".
"There is a definitive improvement in relations and cooperation between police is excellent," Delgado said.

In the past, Basque guerrillas hid in the Pyrenees mountain range in the Basque region of southern France, exploiting the lack of coordination between the two security forces to hide arms and plot activity in Spain.

But French police have become increasingly aggressive at ferreting out ETA strongholds on their territory in recent months, and have dealt what Spanish officials see as several major blows to the rebels, who are now retaliating.
